city.name: Shanghai
city.subtitle: Refuge, relief and Jewish life in wartime Shanghai
city.description: Follow the institutions and streets associated with Baghdadi and Russian Jewish communities and the European refugees who found shelter in Shanghai.

tour.title: Jewish Shanghai: Refuge, Community and Memory
tour.subtitle: Five sites from Ohel Rachel to the Hongkou refugee district
tour.overview: The originally proposed Beijing–Shanghai tour has been narrowed to Shanghai because a single GPS tour cannot span two distant cities and five verified public Jewish-heritage stops were not found in Beijing. This route combines Ohel Rachel with four closely linked Hongkou sites.

stops.title: Ohel Rachel Synagogue
stops.address: 500 North Shaanxi Road, Jing'an District, Shanghai, China
stops.shortDescription: The monumental 1920 synagogue built by Shanghai's Baghdadi Jewish community.
stops.fullDescription: The Sassoon family built Ohel Rachel to serve Shanghai's established Sephardi community. It replaced an earlier synagogue and once held dozens of Torah scrolls. The building survives within an institutional compound and is generally opened only for specially authorised services or visits; the exterior is the reliable public experience.
stops.transcript: Ohel Rachel Synagogue opened in 1920 for Shanghai's Baghdadi Jewish community, whose leading families had built commercial networks linking Bombay, Baghdad, Hong Kong and Shanghai. The Sassoon family financed a sanctuary large enough to demonstrate the community's prosperity and confidence. Its walk-in ark once held many Torah scrolls, while surrounding communal institutions supported education and welfare. Shanghai also had Russian Ashkenazi Jews and, later, refugees from Nazi persecution, so Ohel Rachel represents one important layer rather than the whole Jewish city. After 1949 the building passed into other institutional use. It survives, has received conservation attention and has occasionally opened for authorised Jewish services, but ordinary visitors should not assume entry. View the exterior respectfully and do not challenge guards or photograph restricted areas. Starting here establishes that Jewish Shanghai existed before the refugee crisis: the city already contained organised congregations capable of helping newcomers while also facing their own political and economic upheavals.

stops.title: Shanghai Jewish Refugees Museum and Ohel Moshe Synagogue
stops.address: 62 Changyang Road, Hongkou District, Shanghai, China
stops.shortDescription: The principal museum documenting European Jewish refugees in Shanghai, centred on the restored Ohel Moshe Synagogue.
stops.fullDescription: Established in 2007 and expanded in 2020, the museum uses the former Ohel Moshe Synagogue, objects, reconstructed scenes, testimony and a wall bearing 18,578 refugee names. It explains how European Jews reached visa-free Shanghai and lived alongside Chinese neighbours through war and occupation.
stops.transcript: The Ohel Moshe congregation was founded by Russian Jews and moved into this building in 1927. A decade later, Shanghai became an extraordinary refuge for Jews escaping Nazi persecution because entry did not initially require the immigration visas that were increasingly difficult to obtain elsewhere. Thousands of refugees arrived from Germany, Austria, Poland and other countries. They encountered poverty, unfamiliar language, Japanese occupation and war, but also built schools, clinics, newspapers, cafés and cultural life. The expanded Shanghai Jewish Refugees Museum presents nearly a thousand objects and many individual stories. Its Wall of Names records 18,578 refugees, turning a general rescue narrative into named human lives. The story should not become a claim that arrival was easy or that every institution acted generously. Refugees survived through their own labour, international Jewish relief and relationships with Chinese neighbours who were themselves enduring occupation and violence. Bring a passport for registration, check opening hours and allow time for the full exhibition rather than treating the synagogue as a photo stop.

stops.title: Former American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee Site
stops.address: 119–121 Huoshan Road, Hongkou District, Shanghai, China
stops.shortDescription: The former office of a relief organisation that financed shelters, food, hospitals and other assistance for refugees.
stops.fullDescription: The JDC established a Shanghai office in 1938. From this area it coordinated funds for refugee homes, soup kitchens, medical services and education, working with local committees and other organisations. The building is viewed from the public street and should not be entered without explicit permission.
stops.transcript: The American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee opened a Shanghai branch in 1938 and used offices at 119–121 Huoshan Road. Relief organisations faced an immense task: refugees often arrived with little money, while housing, food and medical needs grew rapidly. JDC funding supported communal kitchens, hospitals, schools and refugee homes, working through local committees and international donations. Assistance could mean the difference between illness and survival, but resources were never unlimited and administrators made difficult choices. This stop helps explain that Shanghai's refuge was not sustained by open borders alone. It required fundraising, organisation, paid and volunteer labour, and cooperation across Jewish communities that differed in language and background. The former office is part of an inhabited streetscape rather than a conventional museum. Observe from the pavement and respect residents. As you walk, imagine information, money and requests moving through these rooms while war made communication with families and donors increasingly uncertain.

stops.title: Huoshan Park Memorial
stops.address: 118 Huoshan Road, Hongkou District, Shanghai, China
stops.shortDescription: A small public park where refugees gathered and where a trilingual memorial marks the wartime designated area.
stops.fullDescription: Built in 1917 as Studley Park, Huoshan Park became a place of rest and meeting for Jewish refugees. A memorial installed in 1994 records the area in which stateless refugees were required to live under Japanese occupation. The park is publicly accessible and remains part of neighbourhood life.
stops.transcript: Huoshan Park offered a small patch of open space in a crowded district. Jewish refugees came here to rest, meet friends and give children room beyond cramped rooms and communal shelters. In February 1943, Japanese authorities proclaimed a ‘Designated Area for Stateless Refugees’ and required many refugees who had arrived since 1937 to live within its boundaries. The area is often called the Shanghai ghetto, although it was not enclosed by walls like Nazi ghettos in occupied Europe. Movement was controlled through permits and the district suffered severe crowding, poverty and wartime bombing. A trilingual memorial installed in 1994 marks this history in Chinese, English and Hebrew. The park still serves local residents, so remembrance shares space with ordinary recreation. That coexistence is appropriate: refugees also tried to maintain ordinary life under extraordinary restrictions. Read the marker, then notice the scale of the surrounding streets. Geography made policy tangible by concentrating thousands of displaced people into a neighbourhood already inhabited by Chinese families.

stops.title: Zhoushan Road Refugee Neighbourhood
stops.address: Intersection of Zhoushan Road and Huoshan Road, Hongkou District, Shanghai, China
stops.shortDescription: Surviving lane houses and streets recalling the shops, homes and cultural life once nicknamed Little Vienna.
stops.fullDescription: Zhoushan and Huoshan roads retain buildings connected with refugee homes, cafés and gathering places. The neighbourhood was shared with Chinese residents experiencing occupation and deprivation. This is a living district, so the tour interprets public streets without intruding into homes.
stops.transcript: The streets around Zhoushan Road were once nicknamed Little Vienna because refugees recreated fragments of Central European urban life through bakeries, cafés, newspapers, theatres and small businesses. The name can be evocative, but it must not hide the Chinese neighbourhood already here. Refugees and local residents lived side by side under Japanese occupation, both confronting scarcity and war. Lane houses were subdivided, families crowded into small rooms, and cultural activity offered income as well as psychological survival. Nearby venues such as the Roy Roof Garden hosted performances and gatherings, while the White Horse Café became a remembered social landmark. Many original functions have disappeared and some sites have been reconstructed or redeveloped, so the streets should be read with historical photographs and testimony rather than romantic imagination. Do not enter residential lanes where access is restricted or photograph people without consent. Ending here returns history to everyday scale: rescue was experienced not only through diplomats and institutions but through rent, meals, work, neighbours and the effort to build a temporary home.
